title: Getting Louis Armstrong out of the Home to play his mother's dance
summary: Buddy persuades Captain Jones to release young Louis Armstrong and his band from the Colored Waifs' Home to play a children's and adult dance, with ticket pricing scheme and crowd of 1,800.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Uh, everybody was talking about Lewis Armstrong. He used to have a little band from the home, and every now and then they'd have a parade on Canal Street, and everybody would be talking about Lewis Armstrong. So, one day me and my mother was sitting in the kitchen, and I just had come from work. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I told my mother, I said, you know, sir, I got a good idea. I said, me and, uh, Captain Jones, the man, the head man at the home is good. I'm gonna see if I can get Cap to let Lewis come out of the home and play a little, uh, dance for you. Yeah. So, Professor, Professor Dave was his, uh, instructor. The old man would teach him how to play. Mm-hmm. And, uh, so I went and seen Cap, and, uh, he told me, sure, buddy. What you want? So, I went there and, uh, I spoke to him, so he said, yeah. So, I went out there, he said, what do you want? I said, well, I'm not got to deposit D that my mother gonna have the D ball. So, she selected D, and I went back there, he said, sure. When you get ready, let's come back here, and I'll make out of paper, and I'll release him under your kit. Mm-hmm. And I took him, and he had a hymn, drum, bass, and a guitar. Mm-hmm. And they didn't know, they didn't know but, but three pieces. Three pieces. They played that first piece, and then they jumped from that first piece to that third piece, and after they would play that, they'd come back to that first piece. Oh. And, uh, from three, I mean from three to six was for the children. Well, the children at that time was different than the children of today. And they didn't sell no strawberries, they didn't sell them but lemonade and oranges and apples. Well, that dance was from three to six for the children.

And from six to four was for the growing ups. Yeah, I see. And that Sunday, at that hall, people going in and out, it was so crowded, eighteen hundred people passed through there. That's right. Wow. And, uh, we decided to, to make it like this. Uh, things was cheaper at that time. Uh, make a cheap, cheap admission, you see. Twenty-eight cents. Uh-huh. So we decided to get a ticket. Now, if you get one of these tickets, with this ticket, it is, uh, thirteen cents.

Without the ticket, it's twenty-eight cents. Uh-huh. You see, and that's where we draw the crowd. Everybody was running around looking for a ticket to save that thirteen cents. See, that was a good scheme. Oh, she did wonderful. Sounds like a good scheme. Yeah. What was your mother's name? Effie Two-Rolls. Effie?
